parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Successive ionisation energies for element **A** are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| ionisation | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th | 7th | 8th |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ionisation energy / $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ | 1310 | 3390 | 5320 | 7450 | 11 000 | 13 300 | 71 000 | 84 100 |

Use Table 1.1 to deduce the group of the Periodic Table that **A** belongs to. Explain your answer.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Across Period 3 there is a general trend for first ionisation energies to increase due to the increase in attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron.

Explain why the first ionisation energy of sulfur is less than the first ionisation energy of phosphorus.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
In an $\text{Al}^{2+}$ ion the nuclear attraction for the outer electron is stronger than in an atom of $\text{Na}$.

Compare the electronic structures of $\text{Al}^{2+}$ and an atom of $\text{Na}$ and explain why the third ionisation energy of aluminium is greater than the first ionisation energy of sodium.

parts.label: (e)
parts.text:

Complete Table 1.2 for an atom of copper-65.

parts.label: (f)(i)
parts.text:
The element copper has a relative atomic mass of 63.5.

Calculate how many atoms are present in $1.05\text{ g}$ of copper.

parts.label: (f)(ii)
parts.text:
Copper has a melting point of $1085^{\circ}\text{C}$ and a high electrical conductivity.

Explain these properties of copper by referring to its structure and bonding.
